paragraphs.text: [Zhen Pin](zhen-pin:definition), 珍品, means "precious item". On a [Tieguanyin](tieguanyin:definition) it is the seller's word for a lot set above the ordinary. It is not one of the grades in the [national standard](zhen-pin:how-graded) for Anxi Tieguanyin, which runs from special grade down to third grade. So it marks what this seller counts among its better teas, not a rank shared across the trade.

The leaf grew in [Anxi](anxi:where-it-is), a county of hills and ridges in the south of Fujian, inland from the coast in Quanzhou prefecture. Its weathered granite breaks down into an acidic soil that drains freely, the kind tea likes, and farmers work it in [terraced gardens](anxi:why-tea) below forested ridges. Anxi on a label is a [protected name](anxi:on-a-label). It states where the leaf grew, not its style or its grade.

Tieguanyin is both a cultivar and the [oolong](oolong:definition), a partly oxidised tea, made from it. The leaf is withered, then shaken, which bruises its edges red. Then it is fixed and [wrapped in cloth and rolled](tieguanyin:making) again and again. Each round presses it tighter, until it sets into the tight balls of this tea.

brewing.text: Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: In the light style: orchid and other flowers, a fresh, clean cup and a sweet aftertaste. In the roasted style: toast and charcoal, caramel or honey, stone or dried fruit, nuts, and a liquor that runs from gold to amber.
